questions.stem: The nurse assesses a newborn one minute after birth: heart rate 110, slow and weak cry, some flexion of the extremities, grimace when suctioned, and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What Apgar score should the nurse assign?

options.label: A
options.rationale: A score of five undercounts the findings; each of the five categories earns at least one point here and the heart rate earns two.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Heart rate above 100 scores two; weak cry, some flexion, grimace and acrocyanosis each score one, for a total of six.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Eight would require a strong cry, active motion or completely pink color, none of which were observed.

questions.teachingPoint: Apgar scores heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability and color from zero to two each; seven to ten is reassuring.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client with no family history of cancer asks the nurse when colorectal cancer screening should begin. Which response is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Screening for people at average risk should begin now, at age 45
options.rationale: Current guidelines recommend starting colorectal cancer screening at age 45 for adults at average risk, using colonoscopy or stool-based tests.

options.label: B
options.text: Screening is not needed until age 60 unless symptoms develop
options.rationale: Waiting until 60 or until symptoms appear misses the window in which precancerous polyps can be found and removed.

options.label: C
options.text: Screening is only recommended for people with a family history of colon cancer
options.rationale: Family history increases risk and may move screening earlier, but average-risk adults are screened too.

questions.teachingPoint: Average-risk adults start colorectal screening at 45; those with a family history or inflammatory bowel disease start earlier.

questions.stem: The parent of a healthy 9-month-old infant is worried because the infant is not yet walking. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain that most infants walk independently between 12 and 15 months, so this is expected at 9 months
options.rationale: Independent walking typically appears between 12 and 15 months; at 9 months, pulling to stand and cruising are the expected milestones.

options.label: B
options.text: Refer the infant for a developmental evaluation
options.rationale: A referral is not indicated because the infant is within the normal range for gross motor development.

options.label: C
options.text: Suggest using an infant walker to strengthen the legs
options.rationale: Infant walkers are unsafe, cause injuries and do not speed up walking; they should be discouraged.

questions.teachingPoint: Know the milestone windows: sitting without support around 6 to 8 months, pulling to stand around 9 months, walking around 12 to 15 months.
